Biliary Stricture Management: ESGE Guideline
  • Source: Endoscopy, Vol. 58, 2026 (Published online 2026-09-03)
  • Topic: Management of biliary strictures - endoscopic treatment approaches
  • Author(s): Lemmers A, et al. (14 co-authors)
1. Benign Biliary Strictures
1.1 Postcholecystectomy BBS
  • Incidence: <1% of cholecystectomy cases
  • Location: ~50% involve main hepatic confluence
  • MPSs --> first-line treatment for postcholecystectomy BBS
  • FCSEMS --> alternative when stricture >2 cm from hilum or patient noncompliant with repeated ERCPs
  • MPS protocol: maximum stents, exchange every 3–4 months, total duration 12 months
  • FCSEMS protocol: 8–10 mm diameter, indwell 6–12 months
  • Long-term (5-year) biliary patency: PCSEMSs 81.7% vs MPSs 71.9% (p=0.02)
  • Recurrence rate with MPSs: 9.4% after mean 11-year follow-up
  • FCSEMS migration rate: 16.7%, AE rate 38.9%
  • Conditional recommendation, very low quality evidence
1.2 Post-Liver Transplant: Anastomotic Strictures
  • Incidence after orthotopic liver transplantation: 4%–20%
  • Two treatment options:
  • MPSs: exchange every 3–4 months, 1-year treatment
  • FCSEMSs: 10 mm diameter (8 mm acceptable), indwell 6 months
  • FCSEMS advantages: fewer ERCPs, lower cost
  • ABS resolution similar between FCSEMS and MPSs (meta-analysis)
  • 5-year follow-up recurrence: FCSEMS 36% vs MPSs 7% (RCT data)
  • Another RCT: FCSEMS 51% recurrence vs MPSs at 5 years
  • Intraductal/antimigration FCSEMSs may reduce recurrence
  • MPS simplified protocol (sequential stent addition) --> reduced procedure time, fluoroscopy, cost
  • Conditional recommendation, low quality evidence
1.3 Post-Liver Transplant: Nonanastomotic Strictures
  • Risk factors (7 identified):
  • Deceased cardiac death donor
  • PSC as indication for OLT
  • Roux-en-Y bile duct reconstruction
  • Hepatic artery thrombosis
  • Longer cold and warm ischemia time
  • Total operative times
  • Develops secondary to ischemic cholangiopathy
  • Four types of ischemic cholangiopathy:
  • "Confluence dominant type" --> can be managed with MPSs
  • "Minor form" --> rarely needs stent insertion
  • "Diffuse necrosis" and "multifocal progressive" --> largely stent-dependent, redo OLT often required
  • NBS resolution rate: 41%–60% in retrospective studies
  • Long-term (1–8 years) success rates: 21%
  • Cholangitis during stent program: up to 74% of cases
  • Treatment: balloon dilation + MPSs, exchange every 3–4 months over 1 year
  • Conditional recommendation, very low quality evidence
1.4 Chronic Pancreatitis-Related BBS
  • Stricture resolution after endotherapy: 60%–70% on long-term follow-up
  • Key indications for intervention:
  • Jaundice
  • Cholangitis (prevent progression to sepsis)
  • Prolonged cholestasis (>1 month elevated ALP)
  • FCSEMS (6–12 months) --> preferred over MPSs for chronic pancreatitis BBS
  • FCSEMS advantages: fewer ERCP sessions, larger caliber (equivalent to 6+ plastic stents)
  • RCT data:
  • Ramchandani et al. (164 patients): FCSEMS 75.8% vs MPSs 77.1% stricture resolution at 2 years
  • FCSEMS group required fewer ERCPs (2.6 vs 3.9; p<0.001)
  • Haapamäki et al.: 90% (FCSEMS) vs 92% (MPSs) at 2 years, no significant difference
  • Coté et al.: FCSEMS 92.6% vs MPSs 85.4%, fewer ERCPs (p<0.001)
  • Meta-analysis conclusion: no differences in stricture resolution, AEs, or mortality
  • 5-year follow-up after FCSEMS removal: 61.6% remained stent-free
  • Conditional recommendation, low quality evidence
1.5 Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC)-Related BBS
  • High-grade stricture definition: 75% reduction in duct diameter on MRCP
  • Balloon dilation alone --> preferred for PSC high-grade strictures
  • No added benefit from stenting after balloon dilation
  • Stenting may increase risk of adverse events (mainly cholangitis)
  • Meta-analysis comparison:
  • EBD alone: clinical success 86.5% vs stenting 70.8% (p<0.001)
  • Technical success: 96.8%
  • AE rate: EBD alone 11.2% vs stenting 26.9%
  • RCT (Ponsioen et al.): recurrence-free rate equal between EBD and stenting
  • Severe AEs significantly higher with stent group: 45.4% vs EBD 6.7% (p=0.01)
  • When stenting needed: use plastic stents, remove within 1–2 weeks
  • Conditional recommendation, low quality evidence
2. Malignant Biliary Strictures
2.1 Distal MBO: Preoperative/Neoadjuvant Drainage
  • Avoid USEMS for extrahepatic biliary obstruction of unconfirmed etiology
  • Conditional recommendation, low quality evidence
2.1.1 Preoperative Biliary Drainage (PBD)
  • Indications for PBD:
  • Cholangitis
  • Severe symptomatic jaundice (e.g. intense pruritus)
  • Delayed surgery after 2 weeks
  • Before neoadjuvant chemotherapy in jaundiced patients
  • Routine PBD may be avoidable when upfront surgery planned within 1–2 weeks
  • Landmark RCT (van der Gaag): PBD increased severe AEs (74% vs 39%) but no difference in surgical complications
  • SEMS preferred over plastic stents for PBD (lower dysfunction rates)
  • Meta-analysis (12 studies, 683 patients): SEMS vs plastic stents
  • Longer stent patency with SEMS
  • Fewer endoscopic reinterventions
  • More post-ERCP AEs (PEP 10.7% vs 4.7%)
  • Modified FCSEMS vs plastic stents: reduced AEs (6.9% vs 27%, p=0.04), reduced reintervention (0% vs 20.7%)
  • Strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence
2.1.2 Neoadjuvant Biliary Drainage
  • RCT (67 patients): FCSEMS vs plastic stents
  • Less stent dysfunction: 18.2% vs 72.8% (p=0.02)
  • Fewer reinterventions
  • Lower AE risk with SEMS
  • RCT (119 patients): FCSEMS vs USEMS for neoadjuvant PBD
  • Similar biliary drainage, reintervention, and AE rates
  • 4-cm stent was predictive of need for reintervention --> prefer 6-cm SEMS
  • Strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence
2.2 Distal MBO: Palliative Drainage
  • Endoscopic over surgical or percutaneous biliary drainage for primary decompression of inoperable MBO
  • Strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence
2.3 Stent Choice for Palliative Distal MBO
  • SEMS insertion recommended for palliative drainage of confirmed extrahepatic MBO
  • Strong recommendation, high quality evidence
  • Covered vs uncovered SEMSs: no differences in stent dysfunction, reintervention, or survival
  • Innovations to decrease migration/ingrowth:
  • Coaxial double-pigtail stent insertion --> reduces FCSEMS migration from 40% to 15%, prolongs patency from 173 to 237 days
  • Multihole SEMS --> less recurrent biliary obstruction (21%), less ingrowth (13%), less migration (2.6%)
  • Modified FCSEMSs with antimigration features --> lower migration, longer patency
  • PCSEMS vs FCSEMS meta-analysis (62 studies):
  • Time to recurrent biliary obstruction: PCSEMS 369 days vs FCSEMS 238 days
  • AE rate not different
2.4 EUS-BD for Primary Palliative Distal MBO
  • Meta-analyses (RCTs) comparing EUS-BD vs ERCP: similar technical success, clinical success, safety, stent patency
  • EUS-BD using LAMSs showed superior technical success in some RCTs (due to low ERCP success rate in one study: 76%)
  • Real-world data:
  • Technical failure rate: 7%
  • Risk factors: CBD ≤15 mm, low operator experience (≤10 LAMS placements)
  • 30-day mortality: 12%
  • CBD diameter ≥12 mm preferred for EUS-BD
  • Only 6.6% of distal MBO cases needed EUS-BD as primary drainage (high-volume center data)
  • Conditional recommendation, low quality evidence
2.5 Hilar Malignant Strictures: Preoperative Drainage
  • Perform in high volume centers with dedicated hepatobiliary MDT
  • Strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence
  • Routine PBD not recommended for hilar obstruction
  • ERCP preferred over PTBD for preoperative drainage
  • Strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence
  • Conditional recommendation against routine PBD (low quality evidence)
2.6 Hilar Malignant Strictures: Palliative Drainage
2.6.1 ERCP vs PTBD for Hilar MBO
  • Meta-analysis (11 studies): PTBD had superior therapeutic success (OR 3.5, 95%CI 2.1–6.0)
  • Main limitations: mostly retrospective, majority Bismuth III–IV (74%), only 30% bilateral drainage
  • RCT (Coelen et al., closed prematurely): PTBD higher mortality (41% vs 11%, RR 3.7)
  • Retrospective bicenter study (Lubbe et al., 293 patients):
  • Similar technical success: 98% vs 99%
  • ERCP had more sustained drainage (3-month gain)
  • PTBD higher procedure-related death: 15.8% vs 6.0% (p<0.001)
  • Conditional recommendation, very low quality evidence
2.6.2 Drainage Strategy by Bismuth Type
  • Bismuth I–II: ERCP for palliative drainage
  • Bismuth III–IV: ERCP or combination with EUS-BD preferred over primary PTBD
  • Complementary PTBD may be required in some cases
  • Conditional recommendation, very low quality evidence
2.6.3 Target Drainage Volume
  • >50% of viable nonatrophic liver volume for palliative drainage (minimum target)
  • Ideally aim for ≥70% of viable nonatrophic liver volume
  • Use multimodal approach: ERCP +/– EUS-BD +/– PTBD as needed
  • Clinical success correlates with >50% liver drained (OR 4.5, p=0.001)
  • Survival improved with >50% drained: 119 days vs 59 days (p=0.005)
  • More recent data suggest cutoff may be ≥80% for optimal outcomes
  • Patients with ≥80% liver drained: better survival (8.5 months vs 3.5 months, p<0.001)
  • ROC threshold for chemotherapy administration: 71% liver drained
  • Conditional recommendation, low quality evidence
2.6.4 Stent Choice for Hilar MBO
  • Use either plastic stents or USEMSs for palliative drainage of proven malignant hilar obstruction
  • Plastic stent --> when optimal drainage strategy not defined
  • USEMS --> in expert centers to reduce revisional procedures based on:
  • Patient's expected survival
  • Likelihood of achieving complete biliary drainage
  • Conditional recommendation, moderate quality evidence
2.6.5 Unilateral vs Bilateral Stenting
  • RCT (133 patients): bilateral SEMS vs unilateral
  • Similar technical success: 95.5% vs 100%
  • Bilateral had higher clinical success (95.3% vs 84.9%, p=0.047)
  • Bilateral had lower primary reintervention (42.6% vs 60.3%, p=0.049)
  • Median cumulative stent patency: 252 days vs 139 days (favoring bilateral)
  • Systematic reviews: bilateral drainage reduces reintervention, prolongs stent patency
  • Large multicenter retrospective (236 patients):
  • Unilateral technical success higher: 98.8% vs 82.5%
  • Bilateral clinical success higher: 85.7% vs 70.5%
  • Bilateral had reduced postprocedure mortality (HR 0.36, p<0.01)
  • Bilateral had prolonged survival: median 828 vs 202 days
3. ERCP Failure/Unfeasible Cases
3.1 Malignant Biliary Stricture: Failed ERCP without Duodenal Stricture
  • EUS-BD over PTBD recommended when ERCP fails or unfeasible in malignant biliary stricture
  • Strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence
3.1.1 Technical Approach for Distal Stricture
  • No duodenal stricture --> EUS-HGS or EUS-CDS both options
  • Duodenal stricture present --> EUS-HGS preferred
  • EUS-BD fails or not feasible --> use PTBD
3.1.2 Evidence for EUS-BD vs PTBD
  • Four meta-analyses + three RCTs: low quality evidence for EUS-BD with:
  • Similar technical and clinical success to PTBD
  • Reduced AEs (OR 0.25, 95%CI 0.10–0.61)
  • Reduced recurrent biliary obstruction (OR 0.05, 95%CI 0.01–0.25)
  • EUS-HGS and EUS-CDS with SEMS: similar technical and clinical success
  • No RCTs have included EUS-CDS performed with LAMS specifically
3.1.3 Patient Preference
  • International survey (327 patients): >80% preferred EUS-BD over PTBD for ERCP failure
  • Reasons: no percutaneous drain, possibility of one-stage procedure
3.2 Malignant Biliary Stricture: Failed ERCP with Duodenal Stricture
  • Combined biliary and gastric outlet obstruction (double malignant obstruction)
  • EUS-BD over surgical bypass or percutaneous drainage when expertise available
  • Conditional recommendation, very low quality evidence
3.2.1 EUS-HGS vs EUS-CDS in Double Obstruction
  • Pooled analysis (4 studies): EUS-CDS associated with higher recurrent biliary obstruction vs EUS-HGS
  • RR 5.04, 95%CI 2.09–12.14
  • Risk factors for EUS-CDS dysfunction: pyloroduodenal invasion, gastric outlet obstruction, mildly dilated CBD
  • EUS-HGS preferred when duodenal stricture present (farther from tumor site)
  • EUS-guided double bypass (EUS-ge + EUS-BD) vs surgical double bypass:
  • Similar technical and clinical success
  • Significantly reduced AEs (especially severe)
  • Shorter hospitalization
4. Surgically Altered Anatomy Management
4.1 Billroth II Post-Surgery
  • ERCP with front-viewing or side-viewing endoscopes can be considered
  • Conditional recommendation, moderate quality evidence
4.2 Post-Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple)
  • Options: EA-ERCP, EUS-BD, PTBD may be considered
  • For benign biliary strictures: EA-ERCP first-line, EUS-BD for selected cases (multiple interventions expected, difficult index EA-ERCP)
  • For malignant biliary strictures: EA-ERCP or EUS-BD (antegrade or EUS-HGS/EUS-HJS) as first-line, PTBD second-line
  • EA-ERCP success rates: 61.7%–75.8% (SBE meta-analyses)
  • DBE success: 93% in 1323 patients with surgically altered anatomy
  • EUS-BD success: technical 97.8%, clinical 94.9%, AE rate 12.8%
  • Conditional recommendation, low quality evidence
4.3 Post-Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass (RYGB)
  • Options: EDGE or EA-ERCP may be considered
  • For benign biliary strictures: EDGE first-line, unless specific expertise in EA-ERCP
  • For malignant biliary strictures: EUS-BD often preferred (antegrade or EUS-HGS/EUS-HJS), EDGE/EA-ERCP/PTBD also options
4.3.1 EA-ERCP in RYGB
  • Success rates: SBE 61.7%–76.4%, DBE 90%–94%
  • AE rates: SBE 6.5%–6.6%, DBE 4%
4.3.2 EDGE in RYGB
  • Meta-analyses: ERCP success 94%–98%, AE rate 14%–18%
  • Compared to EA-ERCP: EDGE superior efficacy (94.8%–100% vs 66%–66.3%)
  • Faster procedure: 61 vs 169 minutes
  • Shorter length of stay: 1.8 vs 6.9 days
4.3.3 EUS-BD in RYGB
  • Meta-analysis (409 patients): clinical success 94%, AE rate 12.8%
  • Conditional recommendation, low quality evidence
4.4 Post-Partial/Total Gastrectomy with Roux-en-Y Jejunojejunostomy
  • Options: EA-ERCP, EUS-BD, PTBD can be considered
  • For benign biliary strictures: EA-ERCP first-line, EUS-BD for selected cases, PTBD for specific indications (CBD/hepatolithiasis)
  • For malignant biliary strictures: EUS-BD or PTBD as first-line in expert centers
  • Conditional recommendation, low quality evidence
4.5 Post-Roux-en-Y Hepaticojejunostomy
  • Endoscopic over percutaneous biliary drainage (better safety profile)
  • For benign strictures: EA-ERCP or EUS-BD (antegrade/EUS-HGS) viable options
  • For malignant strictures: EUS-BD with antegrade or EUS-HGS recommended as first-line
  • PTBD second-line option for both benign and malignant
  • Conditional recommendation, low quality evidence
4.6 Inaccessible Papilla (Malignant Strictures)
  • EUS-BD over PTBD recommended for malignant biliary stricture after failed/unfeasible ERCP
  • Strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence
4.6.1 Technical Options for Inaccessible Papilla
  • Distal stricture without duodenal stricture --> EUS-HGS or EUS-CDS
  • Distal stricture with duodenal stricture --> EUS-HGS preferred
  • EUS-BD fails or not feasible --> use PTBD
5. Second Attempt After ERCP Failure
5.1 Benign Biliary Strictures
  • EUS-RV over transmural drainage when ERCP fails for benign strictures
  • Conditional recommendation, low quality evidence
5.1.1 EUS-RV Technique
  • Meta-analysis: technical success 77%–86.1%, AE rate 14%
  • Recent retrospective series: 25% technical failure rate
  • Prospective/retrospective for benign strictures: better results (92% technical success)
  • Comparative outcomes (EUS-RV vs percutaneous rendezvous):
  • Similar technical success: 89.2% vs 95.8%
  • Similar AEs
  • EUS-RV had higher pancreatitis (2.5% vs 0.8%) and bile leakage (3% vs 0.6%)
  • Insufficient data to recommend EUS-RV over percutaneous rendezvous
5.2 Malignant Biliary Strictures: Failed ERCP without Duodenal Stricture
  • EUS-guided transmural drainage over PTBD for MBO after failed ERCP
  • Conditional recommendation, low quality evidence
5.2.1 EUS-BD Outcomes
  • Meta-analyses: similar technical/clinical success to PTBD but:
  • Reduced AEs (OR 0.25, 95%CI 0.10–0.61)
  • Reduced recurrent biliary obstruction (OR 0.05, 95%CI 0.01–0.25)
  • EUS-CDS with LAMS: >90% technical and clinical success in recent meta-analysis
  • AE rate ~10% (mostly mild/moderate)
  • Reintervention rate ~12%
  • Caution: 30-day mortality 12% in real-world data
5.2.2 EUS-CDS Considerations
  • Favorable when CBD ≥15 mm (adequate biliary dilatation)
  • Unfavorable with pyloroduodenal invasion, gastric outlet obstruction
  • LAMS dysfunction in 32%–55% of cases after EUS-CDS (follow-up data)
  • Place FCSEMS or coaxial DPPT through LAMS to mitigate dysfunction
5.3 Malignant Biliary Strictures: Failed ERCP with Duodenal Stricture
  • EUS-BD over surgical bypass or percutaneous drainage in setting of double malignant obstruction (biliary + gastric outlet)
  • EUS-HGS associated with reduced risk of recurrent biliary obstruction vs EUS-CDS
  • Conditional recommendation, very low quality evidence
6. Technical Aspects of Biliary Stenting
6.1 Antibiotic Prophylaxis
  • Indicated for:
  • Predicted incomplete biliary drainage
  • Hilar stricture management
  • Immunocompromised patients or PSC patients
  • Cholangioscopy procedures
  • Follow ESGE ERCP-related AE guidelines
6.2 Post-ERCP Pancreatitis Prophylaxis
  • Rectal NSAIDs (100 mg diclofenac or indomethacin) in all patients without contraindication
  • Hyperhydration
  • Prophylactic pancreatic stent placement when indicated
  • Follow ESGE guidelines
6.3 Stent Registry for BBS Patients
  • Maintain registry for patients with biliary stents (especially BBS)
  • Recall patients for stent removal/exchange
  • Forgotten stents may be extremely difficult to remove
  • Scheduled exchange/removal reduces septic complications
7. Environmental Impact Considerations
  • Endoscopic management has environmental impact driven by:
  • Single-use devices
  • Energy for intensive imaging, cautery
  • Long-lasting procedures
  • Extensive sterilization processes
  • Multiple endoscopes sometimes used (back-to-back echoendoscope + duodenoscope)
  • Patient travel to/from hospital: major contributor (45%–80% of total carbon footprint)
  • Repeated regular plastic stent replacements contribute significantly
  • Structured waste recycling beneficial (India: 25.7% vs US: 9–20%)
  • Avoidance of reprocessed ERCP/reusable EUS devices reduces carbon footprint
8. Unmet Needs and Evidence Gaps
  • Most recommendations based on low quality evidence
  • Identified needs for future research:
  • Updated RCTs comparing PBD with SEMS vs upfront pancreaticoduodenectomy (current plastic stent data outdated)
  • High-quality comparative trials on FCSEMSs with antimigration systems for BBS
  • RCTs comparing MPS vs FCSEMS in benign postcholecystectomy BBS management
  • Prospective evaluation of liver volumetry for palliative hilar MBO (survival, chemotherapy access as primary outcomes)
  • RCTs comparing PCSEMS vs USEMS in palliative distal MBO
  • Comparative trials on route of drainage in surgically altered anatomy
  • Reported cohorts on route of drainage after ERCP failure for BBS
